title: Find Smallest Common Element in All Rows
description: Find the smallest value common to every row of a matrix with strictly increasing rows, using a single-pass frequency count.

sections.title: Find Smallest Common Element in All Rows

content.title: Find Smallest Common Element in All Rows

blocks.text: Given an m x n matrix mat where every row is sorted in strictly increasing order, return the smallest value that appears in every row. Return -1 if no such value exists.

blocks.caption: Counting occurrences across all rows, a value present in every row will have a count equal to the number of rows.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","mat[][] (each row strictly increasing, so no duplicates within a row)"],["Output","The smallest value common to all m rows, or -1 if none exists"]]}

blocks.text: Since each row is strictly increasing, every value appears AT MOST ONCE per row. This means a value's total count across all rows directly tells how many DISTINCT rows contain it. A value common to every row must have a count exactly equal to the number of rows, turning "find the common element" into a simple frequency-counting problem.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: The "strictly increasing rows guarantee no duplicates per row" observation is what makes a raw frequency count (rather than a full intersection of sets) sufficient here.

Picture several sorted attendance lists (no repeated names within a single list, since each is strictly increasing). Tallying how many lists each name appears on, a name appearing on every list has a tally exactly equal to the number of lists. The answer is the smallest such name.

blocks.caption: A name with a tally equal to the row count appears on every list.

items: Count occurrences of every value across all rows in a hash map.
A value is common to all rows if and only if its count equals m, the number of rows.
Among all values with count equal to m, return the smallest.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: Only the value 5 has a count of exactly 4 (equal to the number of rows), so it is common to all rows. It is also the only such value, matching the expected output of 5.

A direct approach checks each value in the first row against every other row (via a linear scan or nested loop), returning the first (smallest, since the first row is sorted) value found in all rows. This is correct but can be O(m * n) per candidate in the worst case.

Counting occurrences across the whole matrix in one pass answers "is this value in every row" directly via its count, without needing per-row membership checks. Since each row guarantees no duplicates, the count is exactly the number of distinct rows containing that value.

For each value in the first (sorted) row, check whether it appears in every other row via a linear scan, returning the first one found (since the first row is already sorted ascending, this is also the smallest).

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(m^2 * n)","Each of up to n candidates checks up to m rows, each row scanned in O(n)"],["Space","O(1)","No extra storage beyond loop variables"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Repeatedly rescanning rows for membership is unnecessary once a single counting pass can answer the question for every value at once.

Count occurrences of every value across the entire matrix in a single pass, O(m * n). Then scan the count map once, O(distinct values), finding the smallest value whose count equals m, the number of rows.

items: Build a frequency map over all values in the matrix, O(m * n).
Scan the map for values with count exactly m, tracking the smallest.
Return that smallest value, or -1 if none qualifies.

items: When rows are guaranteed to have no internal duplicates (here, strictly increasing), a raw frequency count across all rows correctly identifies "which rows contain this value" without needing set intersections.
A value common to every row has a count exactly equal to the number of rows, a simple and efficient membership test.
This frequency-counting shortcut only works because of the strictly-increasing guarantee; without it, a proper set-based intersection would be needed instead.

blocks.text: Find Smallest Common Element in All Rows is solved by counting every value's occurrences across the whole matrix in one pass, since strictly increasing rows guarantee no duplicates within a row. A value common to all rows has a count exactly equal to the row count, and scanning for the smallest such value gives the answer in O(m * n) time.
